This is infrastructure that assumes you run an engine, not a chat app.

That positioning is what makes the source worth reading. llama.cpp sells portability by avoiding CUDA abstractions; MLC and TVM compile everything ahead of time; FlashInfer sits deliberately in between — ahead-of-time architecture, just-in-time kernels, per-batch planning, and an autotuner closing the loop. For the bigger picture of where it sits among serving stacks, see the inference index, and for the engine that consumes it most visibly, the vLLM tour.
entry.summary: A source tour of FlashInfer, the kernel library behind vLLM and SGLang: the plan/run wrapper contract, host-side split-KV scheduling, JIT-compiled decode and prefill kernels, paged KV cache appends, cascade merges, and the AutoTuner.

entry.title: GGML Source Tour: The Tiny C Engine That Runs llama.cpp

link.title: GGML Source Tour: The Tiny C Engine That Runs llama.cpp

entry.content:
When we toured llama.cpp, the model layer got the attention — templated attention, KV-cache tricks, speculative decoding. Underneath all of it sits a separate repository that does the actual arithmetic: ggml, the tensor engine written in C that llama.cpp consumes as a library. The same engine also powers Whisper.cpp, Stable Diffusion ports, and a long tail of on-device AI projects, which makes it arguably the most executed piece of inference code on consumer hardware today. If ONNX is the contract for describing models, ggml is one of the most battle-tested answers for running them — without a framework, without Python, and often without a GPU.

The design is refreshingly blunt. One public header declares a vocabulary of tensor ops. A core library builds those ops into a compute graph and plans its memory. A scheduler splits the graph across whatever devices are registered — CPU always, plus CUDA, Metal, Vulkan, SYCL, ROCm and friends. Each backend implements the same op set against its own hardware, with the CPU backend carrying an entire sub-discipline of quantized matrix kernels. Around that sits GGUF, a file container that moves weights from disk to tensors, and a small optimizer for people who want training too.

The map below follows that flow: headers to core, core to allocator and scheduler, scheduler out to three real backends, and the GGUF reader feeding the whole thing.

Overview of ggml: ggml.h declares the op vocabulary; ggml.c builds compute graphs, ggml-alloc.c plans their memory, and the backend registry hands devices to the scheduler, which splits work across the CPU, CUDA, and Metal backends; GGUF files provide quantized weights from disk.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The public surface is ggml.h, L1482, where ggml_mul_mat and hundreds of siblings are declared, plus gguf.h, L84 for the container.
  • The C core turns those calls into a graph: ggml.c, L3362 constructs each op node and ggml_build_forward_expand, L7359 grows the cgraph from an output tensor.
  • Memory is planned before any kernel runs: ggml-alloc.c, L498 creates a graph allocator that packs tensors into buffer chunks.
  • The scheduler takes over at ggml-backend.cpp, L1214, using the device registry (L119) to split the graph across the CPU backend, L3391, CUDA, L1950, and Metal, L550.
  • Weights arrive through gguf_init_from_file, L1017, which parses the GGUF header and tensor table into tensors the graph can consume.

One Header, A Whole Compute Vocabulary

ggml’s API is deliberately C99, and it reads like a dialed-down PyTorch: you allocate a context with a fixed memory pool, create tensors, and chain op constructors. ggml_new_tensor, L836 is the root — everything else is shaped metadata around it. The interesting move is that op constructors like ggml_mul_mat, L1482 don’t compute anything; they allocate a result tensor whose src[] pointers point at the operands. The program you write in ggml is therefore a lazily built DAG, captured in the exact order you call the constructors.

The implementation side in ggml.c, L3362 is mostly bookkeeping — reshape checks, type promotion, op params — but the graph-building half deserves attention: ggml_build_forward_expand, L7359 walks parents depth-first into a flat array of nodes. Execution later is just “for each node in order, dispatch to the backend.” No closures, no VM, no tracing pass — the flat cgraph is the intermediate representation, and it is one of the reasons ggml binaries stay small enough to ship in a phone app.

Memory First: The Graph Allocator

Allocating one buffer per tensor would be fatal for transformer graphs with thousands of nodes, so ggml plans memory like a compiler register-allocates. ggml_gallocr_new_n, L498 builds an allocator over a list of buffer types, and the planning pass walks the graph assigning each tensor an offset inside a chunk — reusing the same bytes for tensors whose lifetimes never overlap. The dynamic allocator (tallocr_chunk, L115) keeps free blocks in size-ordered lists so reuse is a search, not a scan.

The output of that plan is a single ggml_backend_buffer per device, plus a schedule of set/cpy operations. This is invisible in the happy path but explains two things you notice in practice: peak memory is stable across runs (the plan is deterministic), and llama.cpp can report exact VRAM requirements before loading — the answer is simply the size of the plan.

The Scheduler: One Graph, Many Devices

The registry is where hardware enters. ggml-backend-reg.cpp, L119 constructs a static list of backends — CUDA (L121), Metal (L124), Vulkan, SYCL, and more — guarded by which libraries were compiled in. The CPU backend is always present, which is why every ggml program works on a bare laptop.

The scheduler then does the puzzle: ggml_backend_sched_split_graph, L1214 walks the graph and assigns every node to a device, honoring where weights physically live and where inputs are produced. The result is a sequence of splits; ggml_backend_sched_compute_splits, L1865 runs each split on its backend and copies boundary tensors between them. Compare this with IREE, which solves the same placement problem at compile time in MLIR: ggml does it at runtime in plain C, in a few hundred lines, favoring robustness over optimality — and for the mixed CPU/GPU rigs most people actually run, robustness is the right call.

The CPU Backend: Where Quantization Lives

The CPU backend is the oldest and most instructive. Execution begins at ggml_graph_compute, L3391, but the planning matters more: ggml_graph_plan, L2811 walks every node, asks each for its scratch requirements, and sums them into a work buffer plus a threadpool configuration. The dispatch (ggml_compute_forward, L1740) is a giant switch over op types, and matmul — the op that matters — lands in ggml_compute_forward_mul_mat, L1255, which fans rows across threads and calls the inner dot product. Standalone kernels like ggml_compute_forward_add, L654 live in their own file now, evidence of the repo’s slow split from one monolith into modules.

The inner loops are the real story. vec.h, L71 declares ggml_vec_dot_f32 and friends — the SIMD atoms, specialized per architecture in the arch directories. On top sit the quantized formats: quantize_row_q4_0_ref, L113 and quantize_row_q8_0_ref, L276 define block layouts (scales, minima, packed nibbles) that make a 4-bit weight look like a tiny struct of 32 elements. The trick ggml popularized is asymmetric quantization: keep weights at Q4 but requantize activations to Q8 on the fly, so the dot product is pure integer SIMD. When a weight layout benefits from reordering, repack.cpp interleaves blocks into GEMM-friendly tiles with dedicated GEMV kernels (L843) — the same tile-shape obsession you see in FlashInfer, just aimed at SIMD instead of tensor cores. And for servers with Sapphire Rapids silicon, the AMX path (ggml_amx_init, L214) requests tile-data permissions and provides its own buffer type — the technique KTransformers leans on for its CPU-heavy MoE offload.

GPU Backends: CUDA and Metal

The CUDA backend mirrors the CPU structure but swaps the hard parts. Device enumeration happens once in ggml_cuda_init, L265; op dispatch lands in ggml_cuda_mul_mat, L1950, which chooses between three regimes: for a single token against quantized weights, the vectorized kernel in mmvq.cu, L601 dequantizes in registers; for larger batches, ggml_cuda_mul_mat_q, L134 requantizes activations to Q8 and runs tiled integer matmuls from shared memory; for dense FP16 it falls back to tensor-core GEMM. Attention is separate and equally tiered — ggml_cuda_flash_attn_ext, L757 picks between an MMA variant for long contexts and a scalar vector variant for short ones. The graph-level entry (L4684) wraps all of it and, when the graph is safe, replays it on a CUDA graph to shave launch overhead.

Metal follows the same shape with Apple flavor: ggml_backend_metal_graph_compute, L550 encodes kernels onto command buffers, while ggml-metal-common.cpp, L35 hosts the kernel-choice heuristics — when a matmul is small enough for the matrix-accelerator path (L143) versus a plain SIMD path. Reading CUDA and Metal side by side is the best way to see what a “backend” really is: the same op list, two entirely different engineering cultures.

GGUF and the Training Loop

The container is what makes the ecosystem shareable. gguf.h, L84 declares the reader; gguf_init_from_file, L1017 (with the I/O in init_from_file_ptr, L966) parses a magic number, a version, a key-value metadata section, and a tensor table of (name, type, dimensions, offset) records. Weights are memory-mapped or read straight into buffers typed by the same block layouts from the quantization section — which is why a Q4_K_M GGUF produced by one tool loads identically everywhere. Contrast with the protobuf world of ONNX: GGUF bet on a simple binary footer and mmap-friendly layout, and for single-file LLM weights that bet has largely won.

Less known: ggml ships training too. ggml_opt_init, L549 builds static forward and backward graphs for a dataset shape, and ggml_opt_epoch, L881 runs the train/eval loop with callbacks — the machinery behind llama.cpp’s LoRA fine-tuning tools. Gradient support flows through the same graph builder we saw earlier (L7359), with each op carrying an optional backward function.

From Install to Your First Model

ggml builds with plain CMake — no Python, no package manager beyond your compiler:

git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml
cmake -B build -DGGML_NATIVE=ON && cmake --build build --config Release

And a minimal C program computes y = W·x end to end — graph, allocator, scheduler, backend:

#include <ggml.h>
#include <ggml-alloc.h>
#include <ggml-backend.h>
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    struct ggml_init_params ip = { 2 << 20, NULL, true };
    struct ggml_context * ctx = ggml_init(ip);

    int64_t nw[2] = {2, 2}, nx[1] = {2};
    struct ggml_tensor * w = ggml_new_tensor(ctx, GGML_TYPE_F32, 2, nw);
    struct ggml_tensor * x = ggml_new_tensor(ctx, GGML_TYPE_F32, 1, nx);
    struct ggml_tensor * y = ggml_mul_mat(ctx, w, x);

    struct ggml_cgraph * gf = ggml_new_graph(ctx);
    ggml_build_forward_expand(gf, y);

    ggml_backend_t cpu = ggml_backend_cpu_init();
    float wd[4] = {1, 2, 3, 4}, xd[2] = {1, 1};
    ggml_backend_tensor_set(w, wd, 0, ggml_nbytes(w));
    ggml_backend_tensor_set(x, xd, 0, ggml_nbytes(x));
    ggml_backend_graph_compute(cpu, gf);

    float out[2];
    ggml_backend_tensor_get(y, out, 0, ggml_nbytes(y));
    printf("%f %f\n", out[0], out[1]);  // 3.0 7.0
    ggml_free(ctx);
    return 0;
}

Twenty lines, and every layer of the map is exercised: context and tensors from ggml.h, graph building from ggml.c, allocation through the no-alloc context, execution through the CPU backend. Swap ggml_backend_cpu_init() for a CUDA device from the registry and the same graph runs on a GPU — that symmetry is the whole point.

Honest Limits and Where ggml Fits

Limits, honestly stated. ggml is a tensor library, not a compiler: there is no kernel fusion across ops, no static shape analysis, no autotuning search — kernels are hand-picked by heuristics, which is why exotic architectures sometimes lose to less famous stacks. The op set is shaped by transformer serving; convolutions and 2D vision ops exist but are not the center of gravity. Quantization is a zoo by now — Q4_0 through Q8_0, K-quants, I-quants — and choosing among them requires llama.cpp wiki knowledge that the ggml repo itself only partially documents. And the C API, while stable in practice, moves with llama.cpp’s needs; it is a library evolving inside a product, not a spec committee’s deliverable like ONNX.

For fit: read ggml when you want to understand what inference actually costs — a matmul is rows times threads times dot products, no more — or when you need to embed inference in something with no Python runtime. It also completes the mental model of our other tours: ONNX Runtime and Triton Inference Server show the serving view, MIGraphX and IREE show the compiler view, and ggml shows the machine view. All of them, plus the rest of the inference catalog, eventually reduce to what ggml does with zero ceremony: build a graph, plan the memory, split it across devices, and multiply.
entry.summary: A guided walk through the ggml repository: the header that defines a compute vocabulary, the graph allocator, the device scheduler, the CPU backend where quantization lives, the CUDA and Metal backends, and the GGUF container that feeds them.

entry.title: IREE Source Tour: One MLIR Compiler Stack From PyTorch Graph to Every Device

link.title: IREE Source Tour: One MLIR Compiler Stack From PyTorch Graph to Every Device

entry.content:
Most inference projects we have toured pick one strategy and sharpen it: vLLM optimizes GPU serving, llama.cpp squeezes CPUs, KTransformers splits work across both. IREE (Intermediate Representation Execution Environment) takes the hardest and most general path: a full compiler stack, built on MLIR, that lowers a machine-learning program through four increasingly machine-specific dialects and then executes it on CPUs, AMD GPUs via HIP, NVIDIA GPUs via CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, and even microcontrollers — from one source tree. If MIGraphX is a compiler with one vendor target, IREE is the same idea stretched across an entire industry, and its repository is the best public classroom for what “ML compiler” really means.

The key to reading IREE is a single boundary. Everything above it is compile time: MLIR code that transforms other code. Everything below it is runtime: C code with no MLIR dependency at all that loads compiled artifacts and runs them. The seam is the Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) — a dialect on the compiler side, a driver model on the runtime side. Once you see that, the four-dialect pyramid stops being alphabet soup: Flow shapes the work, Stream schedules it in time, HAL names the machine, VM carries the host program.

The overview below follows that pyramid down and then crosses the seam into the runtime, where a driver registry hands out devices and a bytecode VM executes the compiled module.

Overview of IREE: the Flow, Stream, HAL, and VM dialects form the compile-time pyramid; compiler stages orchestrate the transformations; at runtime, a driver registry instantiates HIP or CPU devices, executable caches hold compiled binaries, and the bytecode VM runs the serialized host program.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The Flow dialect (FlowOps.cpp, L1256) partitions tensor work into dispatch regions; the Stream dialect (StreamOps.cpp, L3479) then wraps them into async execution regions with explicit fences.
  • The HAL dialect (HALOps.cpp, L1683) names devices, command buffers, and executables, while host-side control logic lowers to the VM dialect (VMOps.cpp, L148).
  • The compile stages are orchestrated top-down from a single compiler entry point and materialized by the dialect-level pass builders — the HAL transforms (Passes.cpp, L310) resolve target backends through TargetRegistry.cpp, L100.
  • Across the seam, driver_registry.c, L89 registers driver factories — the HIP driver (hip_driver.c, L114) among them — and executable_cache.c, L76 prepares compiled code per device.
  • The bytecode module (module.c, L892) loads the serialized VM program, and iree-run-module-main.c, L92 is the reference CLI that exercises the whole chain.

The Four-Dialect Pyramid

IREE’s compiler is a pyramid of MLIR dialects, each existing to answer one question the previous one left open. Flow asks “what work is there?” Its dispatch builder (FlowOps.cpp, L1256) traces tensor dependencies and carves the program into dispatchable regions — the unit of work every later stage manipulates. Verification like DispatchWorkgroupsOp::verify, L890 enforces that each region captures exactly what it needs, nothing more.

Stream asks “when does the work happen?” AsyncExecuteOp::build, L3479 wraps dispatches into async execution regions with explicit waits and signals, making concurrency a property of the IR rather than a hope. The Stream transforms (Passes.cpp, L178) then schedule, allocate, and elide redundant state — this is where IREE decides that two independent dispatches can overlap on the device.

HAL asks “what machine runs it?” ExecutableOp::build, L1683 wraps target-specific code objects, and CommandBufferDispatchOp::build, L1405 records dispatches the way a GPU command buffer would. The HAL transforms (the device-configuration stage at L245, main sequence at L310) assign devices, materialize interfaces, and hand executables to backend codegen selected via getTargetBackend, L100. Backends register themselves through mergeFrom (L30) — a plugin architecture that lets the LLVM-CPU, CUDA, HIP, Vulkan, and Metal generators live as swappable modules.

Finally the VM dialect asks “what does the host do between launches?” FuncOp::build, L148 and module verification (L110) produce a small register-based program that serializes to a flatbuffer — the .vmfb file IREE deploys. Everything else got compiled away; the VM keeps only control flow, function calls, and the glue that talks to devices.

Across the Seam: Drivers, Caches, Devices

The runtime never sees MLIR. It sees the HAL C API: drivers, devices, command buffers, executables. driver_registry.c, L89 stores statically registered factories, and device queries fan out across them (L209) so callers can enumerate “give me every HIP GPU” without knowing vendor details. Each driver is a self-contained directory under runtime/src/iree/hal/drivers/.

The CPU story has two flavors, and the contrast is instructive. The multithreaded device (task_device.c, L272) creates task queues and pools (L129) so dispatches run asynchronously across cores — this is the driver that makes CPU inference scale. The synchronous device (sync_device.c, L160) executes every command inline on the calling thread: simpler, slower, and the right choice for embedded or single-threaded hosts. On the GPU side, the HIP driver (hip_driver.c, L114) loads vendor symbols dynamically and manages streams, events, and device parameters.

Compiled code lands in the executable cache: create, L31 makes one per device, can_prepare_format, L67 asks whether a binary format is understood, and prepare_executable, L76 turns serialized compiler output into live code. This is the mechanism behind IREE’s cached-deployment story — compile once on a build machine, ship the artifact, load it on the target with zero JIT. Readers of our TVM and Executorch tours will recognize the same ahead-of-time philosophy; IREE’s version is unusual in that the host program is compiled too, not just the kernels.

The rest of the HAL runtime is the machinery every device shares through those vtables. Command buffers record dispatches, copies, and barriers into device-specific backends — the HIP driver, for instance, offers both immediate stream recording and CUDA-graph-style capture so a whole command sequence can be replayed with a single launch. Fences and semaphores give the compiled program a way to express the same wait/signal structure the Stream dialect baked into the IR, which means the runtime never has to guess ordering: it executes exactly the dependency graph the compiler decided. Allocators round it out with buffer pools sized at device creation, keeping steady-state inference free of per-step allocation churn — the same discipline our FlashInfer and KTransformers tours found inside their respective schedulers, here generalized behind one interface.

The VM: A Tiny Interpreter With a Big Job

The .vmfb artifact contains a flatbuffer archive of the VM program plus any embedded data. Bytecode module creation at L892 parses and verifies the archive header, and function lookup (L275) resolves exported names. Execution is a compact register machine: dispatch_begin, L1124 enters the interpreter loop, where each opcode is a small C handler — branch, call, or invoke a native import.

Native imports are how the VM talks to devices. The HAL module (module.c, L2139) exposes hal.* functions — buffer creation, command buffer recording, dispatch submission — that the compiled host program calls. When the interpreter hits hal.command_buffer.dispatch, it walks through the device vtable of whichever driver the session selected, which is how one .vmfb file runs unchanged on HIP, CPU, CUDA, or Vulkan. The same trick hosts our KTransformers friend SGLang’s CPU backends elsewhere; here it is the entire portability contract.

From Install to Your First Model

IREE builds with CMake and ships Python wheels (pip install iree-compiler iree-runtime on supported platforms). The quickest end-to-end tour uses the CLI tools:

# compile an MLIR/ONNX-sourced program to a .vmfb for the CPU
iree-compile model.mlir --iree-hal-target-backends=llvm-cpu -o model.vmfb

# run it on the local-task CPU driver
iree-run-module --device=local-task --module=model.vmfb \
  --function=predict --input="1x3x224x224xf32"

# same artifact, HIP driver, no recompile
iree-run-module --device=hip --module=model.vmfb --function=predict \
  --input="1x3x224x224xf32"

iree-run-module (main at L92) is deliberately boring: it builds a runtime session (session.c, L66), loads the bytecode module, parses inputs, invokes, and prints. That boringness is the point — the session API it exercises is the same one embedders use, and the demo directory in the runtime source has a fully annotated hello-world that explains every call. For tracing, the companion iree-dump-instruments and tracy tooling expose per-dispatch timings on device.

Honest Limits and Where IREE Fits

Limits first. IREE is a compiler stack, so its floor is higher than a runtime’s: integration means build systems, target flags, and understanding where your model’s ops land in the pyramid — the project’s own docs warn that frontend coverage (PyTorch via StableHLO paths, ONNX import) evolves continuously, and exotic ops can force you into custom dispatch work. Performance for large-scale LLM serving on NVIDIA GPUs is not its center of gravity; the vLLM-class stacks we covered — vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM — own that niche with far more serving machinery. And the HAL’s generality has a cost: peak single-vendor performance usually requires the vendor’s own library path, which is precisely what MIGraphX and FlashInfer optimize for their respective ecosystems.

As for fit: IREE is the right study object and increasingly the right tool when your deployment target list is long and unforgiving — mobile and edge devices, heterogeneous servers, safety-conscious embedded systems — and you want one artifact story across all of them. It is also, frankly, the best way to learn what a modern ML compiler does, because the four-dialect pyramid makes each transformation step legible. Between the compile-time IR layers and the deliberately MLIR-free runtime, IREE demonstrates the same lesson our inference overview keeps returning: the interesting engineering is almost always at the boundary where a portable abstraction meets hardware that refuses to be abstract.
entry.summary: A guided walk through IREE: the four-dialect MLIR pyramid (Flow, Stream, HAL, VM), the HAL seam between compile time and runtime, drivers for CPU and HIP, the bytecode VM, and the tooling that ties it together.

entry.title: KTransformers Source Tour: How kt-kernel Runs Giant MoE Models on CPU Plus GPU

link.title: KTransformers Source Tour: How kt-kernel Runs Giant MoE Models on CPU Plus GPU

entry.content:
KTransformers earned its reputation by doing something that sounds impossible: running DeepSeek-class mixture-of-experts models on a workstation GPU paired with a big pile of ordinary DDR memory. The trick is placement, not magic — dense, attention-critical work lives on the GPU, while the enormous expert feed-forward layers, which see only a few experts per token, stream from CPU RAM through heavily optimized kernels. A README benchmark line puts DeepSeek-R1-0528 (FP8) at 227.85 tokens/s total throughput and 87.58 output tokens/s at 8-way concurrency on 8×L20 GPUs plus a Xeon Gold 6454S. If you have followed our earlier CPU-inference tours of llama.cpp and BitNet, this project sits at an interesting midpoint: llama.cpp keeps everything on CPU, while KTransformers treats the CPU as a first-class co-processor beside the GPU.

There is a second reason this tour is timely. The repository rebuilt itself. Today’s live tree is kt-kernel, a slimmer C++/Python library whose README promises “CPU-optimized kernel operations for heterogeneous LLM inference” plus a fine-tuning track with LlamaFactory. The historic Python servers — the OpenAI-compatible API, the balance-serve scheduler, the old kvc2 prefix cache — now live under archive/, preserved but no longer the point. Reading the old tree to understand the new one wastes effort, so this walk sticks to the files that ship today. That also makes KTransformers a useful contrast to our DeepSpeed coverage: DeepSpeed moves tensors to CPU as an offload afterthought, while kt-kernel was designed around the CPU from the first line.

The map below shows the whole engine. A thin Python CLI and loader family hand weights to a pybind11 bridge; the bridge exposes operator interfaces implemented twice — once with Intel AMX tiles, once in portable AVX2 — while a paged KV cache serves Quest-style sparse attention, and a NUMA-aware worker pool keeps dozens of cores fed.

Overview of kt-kernel: the Python frontend and loaders feed the native bridge; operator interfaces dispatch to AMX or AVX2 expert kernels and the block-sparse attention path, all running over a NUMA worker pool, with CUDA ops handling GPU-side GPTQ and gating.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • kt run (run.py, L85) resolves a model, sanity-checks environment variables, and either boots the engine directly or builds a SGLang command that loads kt-kernel as its CPU expert backend — the same integration path our SGLang tour covered from the serving side.
  • The loader family in loader.py, L816 reads GGUF checkpoints (a format our llama.cpp tour traced back to its C++ origin) and a whole zoo of safetensor precisions, then translates tensor names into kt-kernel’s slots.
  • The native bridge (ext_bindings.cpp, L561) publishes the operator contracts from common.hpp, L418 and stamps __cpu_variant__ attributes onto the module so Python can pick AMX, AVX-512, or AVX2 code at import time.
  • On the GPU side, a separate extension (binding.cpp, L22) registers GPTQ Marlin GEMM, top-k softmax gating, and GGUF dequantization kernels — a vocabulary shared with vLLM, from which the gating kernel is explicitly adapted.
  • Underneath everything, task_queue.h, L22 and worker_pool.h, L138 provide the NUMA-aware execution fabric every kernel runs on.

Now let’s descend into each layer.

A Framework That Rebuilt Itself Around kt-kernel

The first surprise in the repo listing is how small the live surface is. archive/ holds several generations of the old project, including the C++ sources of the original KTransformers servers. The active tree is kt-kernel/, and its shape tells you the architecture story immediately: operators/ for the math, cpu_backend/ for threading, cuda/ for GPU helpers, python/ for the CLI and loaders, plus one top-level ext_bindings.cpp gluing it together.

The Python entry (run.py, L170) shows how deliberately thin the frontend is. _run_impl checks for conflicting environment variables (L586), picks between local serving and delegating to SGLang, and otherwise stays out of the way. This is the opposite philosophy from Triton Inference Server, which owns the whole serving surface; kt-kernel is a kernel library that deliberately lets a real server own the HTTP.

The import-time variant detection is the cleverest bridge detail. ext_bindings.cpp, L565 attaches attributes like "amx", "avx512_bf16", "avx512_vnni", and "avx2" to the module, alongside __int8_weight_layout__ at L583. Python code inspects these flags once and binds the right specialization, so no runtime dispatch tax is paid inside the hot loop. The config structs that flow through the bridge live in common.hpp, L143: a GeneralConfig baseline, QuantConfig at L222, GeneralMOEConfig at L230, and the two abstract contracts — MLA_Interface at L412 and MoE_Interface at L418 — that every backend implementation must satisfy. Nothing in the Python layer knows whether AMX or AVX2 will answer.

CPU MoE Experts: AMX Tiles and the CRTP Stack

The heart of kt-kernel is its mixture-of-experts execution on CPU, and the AMX path is the flagship. Intel’s Advanced Matrix Extensions add tile registers and TMUL dot-product instructions; exploiting them requires weights staged in exactly the right layout. The class hierarchy uses curiously-recurring templates: AMX_MOE_BASE, L39 provides the shared machinery, and each quantization flavor derives from it, while AMX_MOE_TP, L82 wraps per-NUMA-partition instances behind the tensor-parallel facade of TP_MOE at L427.

Weight loading is half the performance battle. load_weights, L263 repacks raw quantized expert bytes into the tile layout AMX demands, with integrity checks like verify_load_right at L154 to catch silent layout corruption. The B-side tile construction lives in amx_buffers.hpp, L499, where BufferBInt4Impl copies each 16×16 tile and applies the VNNI transpose (self-inverse, so the same routine handles both directions) visible at L704. On the A side, BufferAImpl, L20 stages activations with k-group variants for different block-quantized weight shapes.

The forward pass is two GEMMs. do_gate_up_gemm, L238 projects each token’s hidden state through the selected experts’ gate and up matrices, then applies SwiGLU in AVX-512 registers — the activation function sits in amx.hpp, L47, and init_tile at L157 configures the TMUL tile dtypes once per compute type. do_down_gemm, L251 finishes the expert FFN by projecting back down and accumulating into per-partition outputs. Because each NUMA partition owns its own experts’ weights, most memory traffic stays on one socket — which is exactly why the thread pool below matters so much.

For hosts without AMX — AMD EPYC machines, older Intel boxes — AVX2_MOE_BASE, L39 implements the same contract in portable intrinsics, with its own weight staging at L185. The release notes flag AVX2-only support as the path that brought AMD servers into LoRA fine-tuning, and the Python-side wrapper GeneralMoEWrapper, L29 is where a serving framework’s MoE layer gets bound to whichever backend the CPU supports.

Quest-Style Sparse Attention Over Paged KV

Long-context MoE models die on attention long before they die on experts, so kt-kernel’s second pillar is a block-sparse KV cache in the Quest style: keep the full cache, but let each decode step look closely at only the most promising blocks. The manager side is KVCache, L178, sized by KVCacheConfig, L111, with ThreadResize, BatchResize, and BlockResize entry points at L201 through L223 handling the three axes of concurrency.

The attention driver is attn_with_kvcache, L499, which selects between the layer-oriented and KV-head-oriented code paths (the latter starting at attention_kvhead_, L18 for multi-head variants). The sparse sequence then unfolds in four steps. First, quantize_q_, L532 compresses queries to integers so block scoring becomes cheap integer dot products. Second, calculate_block_similarity_layer_, L608 scores every cached block against those queries. Third, select_block_layer_, L737 keeps only the top blocks under the sparsity budget, and retrieval_kvcache_layer_, L799 gathers their K/V pages into a compact working set for the real (full-precision) attention kernel. Finally, calculate_sparsity_layer_, L849 records how much of the cache actually got touched, and get_attn_sparsity, L1514 exposes that number upward so schedulers can adapt budgets.

GPU readers of our FlashInfer tour will recognize the shape of this idea: approximate, structure-aware attention that trades a little recall for a large bandwidth win. The difference is substrate. FlashInfer optimizes what the GPU touches; kt-kernel optimizes what leaves DRAM at all, which on a CPU-bound hybrid stack is the resource that matters.

The NUMA Backend: Queues, Pools, Work Stealing

Every kernel above assumes a pool of workers that understand socket topology, and that fabric is worth its own section. ThreadState, L63 is the per-thread record — cache-line aligned with alignas(64) to stop false sharing, holding core and NUMA node ids plus scratch space. InNumaPool at L72 allocates those states from the right node, and NumaJobDistributor, L105 splits jobs across nodes so an expert computes on the socket that holds its weights.

The WorkerPool, L138 constructor wires it together, init at L159 pins threads, and the escape hatch for uneven work is do_work_stealing_job, L153: when the static NUMA split leaves one socket idling, its threads steal remaining indices from the busy one. Above the pool, TaskQueue, L22 offers the tiny API kernels actually use — enqueue at L27 to submit, sync at L29 to drain — keeping synchronization out of the kernel bodies.

From Install to Your First Model

Installation follows the kernel-library pattern — no service daemon, no config zoo:

git clone https://github.com/kvcache-ai/ktransformers.git
cd ktransformers/kt-kernel
pip install .

kt --help then reveals the CLI surface: run for serving, chat for interactive sessions, bench for throughput, doctor for hardware capability checks, plus quant and sft for the fine-tuning track. A minimal local launch looks like:

kt run --model-path /models/DeepSeek-R1-0528 --gguf-path /models/gguf

The loader negotiates precisions at startup. loader.py, L19 enumerates the GGML quantization types it understands, and the safetensor family covers the modern zoo: FP8 at L332, GPTQ at L1081, MXFP4 at L1198, NVFP4 at L1312, and MXFP8 at L1405. Name translation — mapping a checkpoint’s tensor names into kt-kernel’s expectations — is centralized in translate_name_to_gguf at L89, which is the single most useful file to read when a new model architecture lands.

GPU experts get their weights through the CUDA extension. binding.cpp, L94 registers gptq_marlin_gemm, backed by the warp-specialized Marlin kernel at gptq_marlin.cu, L60 — the same INT4 tensor-core design our vLLM tour saw in production — and binding.cpp, L97 registers topk_softmax, whose fused gating kernel (topkGatingSoftmax, L164) computes softmax, max, argmax, and top-k selection in one launch, adapted from vLLM’s kernels as the file header notes. The placement story this enables is exactly what the README advertises: hot experts on GPU, cold experts on CPU.

The fine-tuning track deserves its own tour, but the shape is worth knowing: KTransformers × LlamaFactory integration lets MoE experts stay quantized on CPU while LoRA adapters train on GPU, and the team reports 6-12× faster training than ZeRO-Offload baselines on the same hardware — a claim we flag as vendor-reported, not independently verified.

Honest Limits and Where kt-kernel Fits

Limits first, since they decide whether this tool belongs in your stack. It is x86-centric: the AMX path needs Sapphire Rapids-or-newer Intel, and while the AVX2 fallback widens coverage to AMD, ARM is off the table for the CPU side. The vendor list in cpu_backend/vendors/ hints at Ascend NPU and HIP ports, but the mature path is CUDA-plus-Intel-CPU. Attention sparsity is approximate — block scoring can miss what full attention would catch, so quality-sensitive deployments should measure, not assume. And the repository is mid-pivot: tutorials and tooling still straddle the old servers and the new kernel, so documentation occasionally points at archive/ paths that are no longer load-bearing.

As for fit: kt-kernel is the answer when model size, not request volume, is your constraint — the single-node case where a 600GB-class MoE model must serve a handful of users on hardware you already own. For multi-tenant serving with routing and batching at scale, the SGLang integration hands those problems to a dedicated server, and for cloud-scale deployments you would compare against the hosted paths in our inference overview or the serving-stack tours of Triton and MLC-LLM. Read it as a specialization of the same lesson llama.cpp taught: when the bottleneck is memory bandwidth, the cheapest spare memory in the building is usually the DIMMs you already have — and KTransformers shows what it takes to make those DIMMs fast.
entry.summary: A guided walk through the kt-kernel source tree: AMX and AVX2 expert kernels, Quest-style sparse attention, a NUMA worker pool, and the CUDA helpers that tie CPU and GPU together.
